content: 1. Zinc acetate is a mineral supplement approved by the FDA for treating patients with Wilson’s disease who have already undergone initial treatment with a chelating agent. 2. In children aged 10 years or older and in pregnant women, a dose of 25 mg of zinc three times daily may be recommended, provided the patient adheres to the therapy. 3. Zinc acetate should be taken on an empty stomach, at least one hour before or two to three hours after meals. 4. Off-label use of zinc acetate in adults has limited guideline-supported information. 5. Patients with rheumatoid arthritis may have impaired zinc absorption, and a 50 mg dose of zinc is often administered. 6. In pediatric patients, off-label use includes zinc gluconate lozenges providing 10 mg of zinc, taken 5-6 times daily, starting within 24 hours of cold symptoms. 7. Infants have been treated with zinc sulfate at 3 mg/kg, achieving complete remission within four weeks. 8. Zinc acetate capsules are contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to any of the formulation’s components. 9. Zinc acetate is not recommended as initial therapy for symptomatic patients due to the delay in its copper-blocking effects. Initial treatment should involve chelating agents. 10. Neurological deterioration may occur during initial therapy as copper stores are mobilized. Maintenance treatment with zinc acetate can be considered once the patient is clinically stable. 11. Adverse reactions reported in Wilson’s disease patients on zinc therapy include gastric irritation, elevated serum alkaline phosphatase, amylase, and lipase levels (suggesting pancreatitis), and rare fatalities due to overdose or advanced liver disease. 12. Zinc acetate has no abuse potential and is not pharmacologically or structurally related to drugs with abuse potential. 13. Studies in pregnant women have not shown an increased risk of fetal abnormalities with zinc acetate or zinc sulfate use during pregnancy. However, it should only be used if clearly needed. 14. Zinc appears in breast milk, and zinc-induced copper deficiency in nursing infants may occur. Women on zinc therapy are advised not to breastfeed. 15. Pediatric patients aged 10 years and above can be maintained on 75-150 mg of elemental zinc daily in divided doses. No studies have been conducted on patients below 10 years of age. 16. There is no FDA guidance on the use of zinc acetate in geriatric patients, specific genders, racial populations, renal or hepatic impairment, or immunocompromised patients. 17. Zinc acetate is administered orally, and therapy should be monitored by assessing signs and symptoms of Wilson’s disease, 24-hour urine copper levels, and liver function tests. 18. Adequate zinc therapy reduces urinary copper excretion to 125 μg per 24 hours or less. A significant upward trend in urinary copper indicates loss of copper control. 19. Plasma non-ceruloplasmin copper levels should be kept below 20 μg/dL. 20. Acute oral overdose with zinc salts is rare. In cases of overdose, unabsorbed zinc should be removed from the stomach via lavage, and chelation therapy should be considered if plasma zinc levels exceed 1000 μg/dL. 21. Wilson’s disease is an autosomal recessive disorder causing copper accumulation in the liver and other organs, leading to hepatic, neurological, and psychiatric symptoms. 22. Zinc acetate works by blocking intestinal absorption and reabsorption of copper, inducing metallothionein production in enterocytes, which binds copper and prevents its transfer into the blood. The bound copper is then excreted in stool. 23. Zinc acetate capsules contain 25 mg or 50 mg of zinc, along with excipients like corn starch and magnesium stearate, in gelatin capsules. 24. Zinc acetate has not been tested for carcinogenicity, mutagenicity, or effects on fertility in long-term animal studies. 25. Clinical studies in Wilson’s disease patients have shown that zinc acetate effectively maintains copper balance and prevents disease progression when used as maintenance therapy after initial chelation. 26. Pregnant women treated with zinc acetate have delivered healthy babies, with no adverse effects on maternal liver or neurological function. 27. Zinc acetate capsules should be stored at 25°C (77°F) with permitted excursions to 15-30°C (59-86°F) in a tight, light-resistant container with a child-resistant closure. 28. Patients should take zinc acetate on an empty stomach, swallow capsules whole, and adhere strictly to the prescribed regimen for optimal copper control. 29. There is no established interaction between alcohol and zinc acetate, but patients should consult their doctor regarding alcohol use with this medication.
